name: Crowd and Ensemble Simulation
title: Crowd and Ensemble Simulation
answer: Crowd and ensemble simulation covers the generation and control of many moving bodies at once, from stadium crowds and street scenes to corps de ballet and marching formations. In choreography and motion mapping it sits between animation and live staging, where a director needs dozens or hundreds of figures to move as a readable whole without losing individual detail. The work spans previsualisation for film and games, stage blocking for large casts, and interactive installations where an audience affects the group in real time.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on game engines and physics middleware, with agents driven by steering behaviours, flocking rules, or learned motion models. Crowd packages such as MassEntity in Unreal and the crowd tools in Unity handle thousands of agents on a single machine, while larger productions distribute simulation across render farms. Motion capture libraries and retargeting pipelines supply the underlying movement, and GPU compute keeps the per-agent cost low enough for interactive playback.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A practitioner typically defines a set of agents, gives each a goal and a set of local rules, then layers global direction on top through flow fields, navigation meshes, or scripted cues. Choreographic intent is expressed as formations, timing markers, and density targets rather than frame by frame poses. Iteration is fast because the same parameters can be replayed, and the results are reviewed in viewport or on stage before being baked for final output.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions arise from the motion data itself, since captured performances may belong to the performers, the studio, or both, and from the use of scanned likenesses in a crowd. Provenance of a simulation is usually recorded as the parameter set, the source motion library, and the engine version, which matters when a shot is reused or a production is audited. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, a reminder that disputes over generated movement and likeness are live rather than hypothetical.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward learned crowd behaviour that responds to direction in natural language and toward real time systems that can drive a stage or a virtual production set without a bake step. Hybrid approaches, where a small number of captured principals steer a larger simulated ensemble, are becoming the default for large scenes. As these tools reach smaller teams, the open questions are less about compute and more about consent, credit, and how a director's intent is documented when the crowd is partly generated.
